In accordance with Section 1.1.2.2 Disclosure Delegated Act (EU) 2021/2178, the numerator equals the part of the
CapEx included in the denominator that is

       1)    related to assets or processes that are associated with taxonomy-eligible or taxonomy-aligned economic
             activities or
       2)    part of a CapEx plan or
       3)    related to the purchase of taxonomy-aligned products.

For Scout24, only assets or processes that are associated with taxonomy-eligible or taxonomy-aligned economic
activities are relevant, as it does not purchase any taxonomy-aligned products, and there are no documented
CapEx plans either in which future investments contribute to aligning existing or new economic activities with the
taxonomy.

Scout24’s CapEx is classified as taxonomy-eligible on account of the following economic activities described in
Delegated Acts (EU) 2021/2139 and (EU) 2023/2486:

       •     CCM44 6.5 Transport by motorbikes, passenger cars and light commercial vehicles
       •     CCM 7.7 Acquisition and ownership of buildings
       •     CE 1.2 Manufacture of electrical and electronic equipment

Taxonomy-eligible economic activities totalled 9.0% in fiscal year 2025 (2024: 17.2%). As a tech company, Scout24's
activities primarily relate to the use or acquisition of assets in sectors H – Transportation and storage (CCM 6.5), L –
Real estate and housing (CCM 7.7) and Manufacture of electrical equipment (CE 1.2) in accordance with NACE. As
these activities were below the materiality threshold of 10% and therefore only contributed to a small extent to
Scout24’s total CapEx, they are reported as immaterial.

OpEx KPI
                                       Taxonomy-eligible or taxonomy-aligned operating expenditure
                      OpEx KPI =
                                                            Direct, non-capitalised costs

The denominator of the KPI related to OpEx in accordance with the taxonomy covers direct, non-capitalised costs
that relate to

       1)    research and development,
       2)    building renovation measures,
       3)    short-term leases,
       4)    maintenance and repair or
       5)    any other direct expenditures relating to the day-to-day servicing of assets of property, plant and
             equipment by the undertaking or third parties that are necessary to ensure the continued and effective
             functioning of such assets.

The numerator is equal to the part of the OpEx included in the denominator that is

       1)    related to assets or processes associated with taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned economic
             activities, including training and other human resources adaptation needs, and direct non-capitalised
             costs that represent research and development or
       2)    part of a CapEx plan or
       3)    related to the purchase of taxonomy-aligned products.

In order to determine the denominator, those accounts in the financial accounting system that reflect direct, non-
capitalised costs were considered. These include the accounts for research and development which, for example,
contain the costs of internal and external employees working in the area of product and platform development.
Accounts for building renovation work, maintenance and servicing were also included. The other building costs
mainly relate to the Company’s headquarters in Berlin. The numerator is derived from an analysis of the taxonomy
eligibility of the assets related to the expenditure recorded in the above-mentioned accounts.

Climate change (ESRS E1)
Transition plan for climate change mitigation (E1-1)
Scout24’s aim is to consistently use renewable energies, reduce energy consumption and minimise emissions from
its operations. The Company believes that the ongoing expansion of Scout24’s product range to include
sustainable products and services is having a potentially positive impact on the end-users of the Company’s
platforms. This may help actively foster climate change mitigation and climate resilience in building stock (for more
information, see }Consumers and end-users), for example. On the other hand, there is the negative impact from
the Scout24 Group’s own operations and by its energy consumption continuing to cause direct and indirect
scope 1, 2 and 3 CO2e emissions that are driving climate change.

Combining the Central Administration & Facility Management and the Sustainability & DEI teams permits efficiently
and effectively pooling the management of environmental and climate-relevant actions, initiatives and processes
and reporting on these directly to the CPSO. The short-, medium- and long-term reduction targets (}Reduction
targets) are part of the }ESG framework and, as such, are integral to the general business strategy and financial
planning. The SBTi officially verified the Scout24 Groups’s medium- and long-term climate targets in the 2025
financial year and published the result on its }website. There are no locked-in GHG emissions associated with the
Company’s key assets or products that could jeopardise the achievement of emission reduction targets. Scout24 is
not exempt from the reference values of the Paris Agreement. The individual parts of Scout24’s transition plan have
been approved by the Management Board.

Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with strategy and business model
(SBM-3)
The analysis of climate-related transitional and physical risks and opportunities identified no assets and business
activities that are incompatible with or need significant efforts to be compatible with a transition to a climate-
neutral economy. Accordingly, no further resilience analysis was carried out.

Policies related to climate change mitigation and adaptation (E1-2)
In this section, the Company reports on the policies it intends to adopt to manage its material impacts related to
climate change mitigation and adaptation.

In July 2021, mobility policies were introduced for employees in Germany and Austria, prioritising rail as a means of
transport and providing for flights only if the journey cannot be made by train within 4.5 hours. Scout24 thereby
reduces the negative impacts of its own employees’ travel activities and the resulting emissions. The policies were
approved by Scout24 SE’s Management Board in Germany and by the management of Immobilien Scout24
Österreich GmbH in Austria. Their implementation is being monitored by the Central Administration & Facility
Management team. The mobility policies’ scope of application covers own operations, i.e. they apply to Scout24
employees, with the exception of the Sprengnetter entities, and to the Management Board and any managing
directors in Germany and Austria. The Sprengnetter entities have their own travel policy that permits air travel
within Germany only in exceptional cases and when travel time exceeds 5.5 hours. It applies to all Sprengnetter
Group45 employees and has been approved by management. Its implementation is monitored by the Internal
Organisation team.

The entire Scout24 Group is also subject to a policy, introduced in 2022, for the sustainable procurement of
advertising materials and event articles that sets out clear guidance. Its purpose is to generally challenge the
procurement of any new advertising materials. If products are nevertheless ordered, the objective is to limit the
range of products considered to those that have been manufactured using renewable or recycled or recyclable
raw materials, contain no harmful substances, have been manufactured under fair production conditions and have
verified labels. This policy also aims to avoid emissions caused by the production of additional advertising
materials and thereby reduce negative impacts on climate change. The policy was authorised by the CPSO and
responsibility for monitoring the policy lies with the Sustainability & DEI team.

Actions and resources in relation to climate change policies (E1-3)
With the aim of further reducing emissions and thus reducing the negative impact on climate change mitigation,
actions have continuously been implemented since the first GHG survey:

    •   As of 31 December 2025, 82.5% (2024: 84%) of Scout24 Groups total fleet consisted of electric cars, 1%
        hybrid vehicles and 16.5% combustion vehicles. The slight deterioration compared to the previous year is
        due to the acquisition of the new subsidiaries bulwiengesa GmbH and neubau kompass AG, as these
        entities previously had scarcely any electric vehicles in their fleets. Over the course of the year, two
        combustion vehicles were replaced by electric vehicles and all new vehicles purchased were electric
        vehicles. So far, the changeover has resulted in a reduction in emissions of 233 metric tonnes of CO2e in
        relation to the base year. Conversion of the entire fleet by the end of 2026 is expected to reduce scope 1
        emissions by 67 metric tonnes of CO2e.
    •   In the 2025 financial year, the amount of energy purchased from non-renewable sources (scope 2) was
        reduced by switching power agreements to renewable energies at four sites. All actions taken since the
        Company started emissions accounting have resulted in a reduction of 435 metric tonnes of CO2e
        (market-based) in relation to the base year 2018. As of 31 December 2025, 14 of the currently 17 office sites
        of all fully consolidated Scout24 Groups entities are being supplied with 100% green electricity. A contract
        change at one of the remaining sites led to a higher specific emissions factor per kWh, which offset part of
        the overall reduction achieved in the reporting year. This site will be discontinued in the course of the 2026
        financial year. At all other sites where Scout24 has a direct influence on the choice of supplier, the
        Company aims to purchase 100% electricity from renewable sources by 2030. This is expected to reduce
        scope 2 emissions by 251 metric tonnes of CO2e.
    •   For one office in Germany, it was possible to convert the contract to biogas as of 1 January 2025. Currently,
        5 of the 17 sites are still heated using natural gas. Three of these sites will be relocated in 2026. Two entities
        will be moving to a new office without natural gas heating, while the third will be assigned to an existing
        site. Since Scout24 started tracking its emissions, the Group has been able to reduce its scope 1 emissions
        by as much as 55 metric tonnes of CO2e in relation to the base year by changing locations or switching
        contracts to biogas.
    •   The reductions in emissions from air travel due to changes in the mobility behavior of employees when
        traveling by air have so far totaled 1,916 tons of CO2e compared to the base year 2018. Air travel is also
        analysed internally during the year in order to identify any increases at an early stage.
    •   Discontinuing the use of in-house data centres in favour of a cloud-based solution has led to cumulative
        savings of around 650 tonnes of CO2e emissions since the base year.
    •   In the 2025 reporting year, the Company began to establish an exchange with its service providers on
        emission data. This way, Scout24 wants to ensure going forward that the most accurate data possible are
        used in calculating the goods and services purchased while also increasing pressure on its supply chain to
        take decarbonisation measures.
    •   In the 2025 financial year, an AI assistant was made available to employees of the Scout24 Group for the
        first time. In addition, since October, Immoscout24 users in Germany have also been offered an AI
        assistant for property searches called HeyImmo. In the reporting period, Scout24 started collecting data
        on the environmental impact of these services in 2025 and plans to publish initial information in 2026.

In 2025, Scout24 began offsetting, as planned, the total emissions of a financial year by means of certified climate
action projects. In accordance with the SBTi Net-Zero Standard, offset GHG emissions are generally not counted
towards target achievement. Instead, they are a voluntary additional contribution to international climate change

Targets related to climate change mitigation and adaptation (E1-4)
In future, the Scout24 Group wants to continue its contribution to keeping the global temperature increase below
1.5°C relative to pre-industrial temperatures. The following targets have been defined in the climate strategy to
reduce the emissions originating from the Company’s operations accordingly:

       1.    Short-term: -60% of absolute CO2e emissions compared to the base year 2018 across all scopes by 2025
       2.    Medium-term: -69.8% of absolute total scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2030 in relation to 2018 and at least a
             -50.4% CO2e reduction in scope 3 emissions in relation to the base year 2018 (scope 3 excluding optional
             categories)
       3.    Long-term: -90% of total absolute scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions by 204546 in relation to the base year 2018
             (scope 3 excluding optional categories)

These targets are based on the requirements of the SBTi Net-Zero Standard for reducing emissions by at least 90%
before 2050. The SBTi officially verified the Scout24 Groups’s medium- and long-term climate targets in the 2025
financial year. The target’s system boundaries correspond to SBTi requirements and therefore include all
mandatory categories. The optional categories under the SBTi approach (hotel accommodation, working from
home, use of products sold), which were nevertheless recorded, are not part of the target. Targets were not
derived based on a sector-specific decarbonisation pathway. For the target, reference is made to market-based
scope 2 emissions. The targets were developed in collaboration with a scientific service provider and taking into
account market insights such as from interviews with investors, approved by the Management Board and
communicated to various other stakeholders including investors, banks and employees.

Scout24 was already able to report a 54% emission reduction across all scopes by the end of 2025. The short-term
reduction target of -60% of absolute CO2e emissions by 2025 compared to the base year 2018 was not achieved,
however. This is primarily due to the following factors:

       •     Entities acquired: the integration of subsidiaries such as the Sprengnetter Group, bulwiengesa GmbH,
             neubau kompass AG and Exploreal GmbH has expanded the accounting basis in recent years, adding the
             emissions of the new consolidated operations.
       •     Structural energy procurement restrictions: as a lessee only, the affiliated companies of Scout24 are
             dependent on the conditions at their respective locations for their energy procurement, including the
             heating systems installed and the contractual framework conditions, which may limit the possibilities for a
             short-term switch to lower-emission energy contracts at individual locations.

When considering scope 1 and 2 emissions separately, there was a reduction of 61% for 2025 compared to the base
year 2018. The reduction in scope 3 emissions was 55% compared to 2018, excluding optional categories. The
medium- and long-term SBTi-validated targets for 2030 and 2045 remain valid and achievable without change.

With these targets, Scout24 SE has committed to continue annual emissions accounting in order to track the
effectiveness of the actions taken and also to continuously identify and implement further potential for reducing
emissions. Achieving these targets requires not only cooperation with all relevant stakeholders and further
technological advances, but also societal change with a successful energy transition. For Scout24, the energy
transition is particularly important for reducing emissions from the use of its platforms, as the data on the number
of sessions on the respective marketplaces, the average length of sessions and the device used are multiplied by
the German electricity mix in order to calculate the corresponding emissions. Further decarbonisation levers are
listed in the }Transition plan for climate mitigation.

Methodology: energy consumption and mix
The figures in megawatt hours (MWh) are taken from supplier invoices, are shown without decimals and have been rounded accordingly. As the full
annual invoices were not yet available for some locations, the missing consumption data were estimated either on the basis of the previous year’s
data or on the basis of the number of square metres of the surface area to be supplied. The share of fossil and nuclear energy was estimated on
the basis of consumption-based average figures for the electricity mix and district heating generation in Germany. The methodology for
determining the energy indicators was further refined in the reporting year. For the first time, the vehicle fleet was systematically included in the
calculation using primary data. The energy metrics were calculated with the help of a scientific service provider and were not additionally
validated by an external body.


Gross scopes 1, 2, 3 and total GHG emissions (E1-6)
Scout24’s corporate carbon footprint (CCF) as presented shows the (gross) GHG emissions for the 2024 and 2025
financial and calendar years. It provides the underlying data for developing the Scout24 climate action strategy
further. Analysing the CCF makes it possible to identify reduction potential and levers, develop suitable actions
and define climate change mitigation targets.

Methodology: accounting boundaries
The calculations are in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (GHG Protocol). As a rule, the
following GHGs listed by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) and in the Kyoto Protocol are included in determining the material
GHGs: carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFC), perfluorocarbons (PFC), sulphur hexafluoride (SF6)
and nitrogen trifluoride (NF3). In the interest of clarity, in the table the material GHG emissions have been converted to CO2 equivalents (CO2e)
using selected emissions factors based on their respective global warming potential. The consumption data recorded (e.g. electricity or fuel
consumption) are converted using emissions factors that indicate the GHG emissions per unit (e.g. per kilowatt-hour or litre). The emission metrics
were calculated with the help of a scientific service provider and were not additionally validated by an external body.

The GHG inventory’s operational boundaries are determined by the Scout24 Group’s consolidation scope. All significant emission categories were
included in the accounting. Emissions in scope 1 and scope 2 include all entities within the consolidated group. Associated companies are
accounted for under scope 3, category 3.15. GHG emissions were generally calculated both location-based and market-based using the dual
reporting procedure pursuant to the GHG Protocol (limited to electricity). The emission factors used for scope 2 and 3 do not differentiate
between fossil and biogenic CO2 emissions, which is why no biogenic emissions are reported for either scope. For 2025, 11% of scope 3 emissions
could be calculated using primary data from suppliers or other partners in the value chain.
In addition to Scout24 SE, the subsidiaries were evaluated according to type of consolidation, share held in the entity, operational control, location
size and number of employees. The GHG inventory’s organisational boundaries are determined by the limitations of the sustainability statement.
Compared to the CCF 2024, the organisational boundary has thus been expanded to include the highlighted entities (‘new’) and their sites.

Since the base year of 2018, the subsequent GHG balances have been continuously developed, completed, and expanded. For the 2025 balance
year, acquisitions led to changes in the organisational balance boundaries. The companies bulwiengesa GmbH, Exploreal GmbH, neubau kompass
AG, and TiRo Check Energy GmbH were newly included or now fully included in the balance boundaries. In addition, there were some changes in
the operational balance sheet boundaries. In order to enable the comparability of emission values and the reduction measures already
implemented since the base year over the following years, the balance sheet frameworks and calculation methods for the individual balance
sheet years were adjusted as part of a recalculation. Of the companies that were part of the CCF 2025, TiRo CheckEnergy GmbH did not yet exist
in the base year and was therefore not included in the recalculation. In order to align the organisational balance sheet boundaries, the emissions
of the existing companies were recalculated on the basis of key figures (full-time equivalents, revenue, office space in square metres). The key
figures for the recalculation were defined per emission category according to the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol and selected according to the
influence of the key figure on the respective category.

The integration of the new subsidiaries led to the following changes in our emissions accounting:

     •     Expansion of the balance sheet boundary: the operational emissions (scope 1, 2, and 3) of the newly acquired companies were
           retroactively included in the base year 2018.
     •     Improvement in data quality through new supplier data: in fiscal year 2025, new data was provided by service providers. For example,
           the cloud service provider now also integrates scope 3 emissions into the company-specific greenhouse gas dashboard, and a major
           online marketing service provider made its own emissions data on the use of online ads available.


These adjustments provide more useful information as they enable consistent comparability across the entire reporting period and accurately
reflect the Scout24 Group’s reduction progress against its climate targets (validated by SBTi). The SBTi-validated reduction targets remain
unchanged, but the base year has been adjusted accordingly.

GHG removals and GHG mitigation projects financed through carbon credits (E1-7)
In accordance with its climate strategy, Scout24 has invested in a gold standard-certified }climate change
mitigation project in Uganda since the 2025 financial year, in parallel to efforts to reduce its own emissions. The
project distributes UV meters and offers training to further the aim of expanding the use of solar water disinfection
in the region. This can help to reduce firewood consumption as well as greenhouse gas emissions, as it eliminates
the need to boil water on open three-stone fires. The amount of the investment covered the total emissions
determined for the 2024 financial year before recalculation, i.e. 3,475 metric tonnes of CO2e. The calculation basis
used for emissions accounting is described under }Gross scopes 1, 2, 3 and total GHG emissions (E1-6). All
certificates (100%) originate from the avoidance project. The certificates do not include a corresponding
adjustment in accordance with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The certificates were cancelled completely. This
investment is not counted towards the carbon footprint and is therefore not a means of achieving the Company’s
climate targets. Rather, it is a voluntary contribution to financing global climate protection, which is intended to
support the mitigation of climate change while the Company continues to drive forward its own climate strategy in
parallel.

The Company is aiming to reduce GHG emissions by 90% by 2045 relative to the base year and plans to then offset
only the remaining 10% of its carbon footprint using carbon credits.



Social information
Own workforce (ESRS S1)
Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with strategy and business model
(SBM-3)
In a technology company such as Scout24, long-term business success largely hinges on the motivation,
productivity and innovative performance of its employees49 and teams, as they implement the Company’s
strategy, identify customers’ and users’ needs and develop new market opportunities. The Scout24 Group
therefore attaches great importance to matters related to employees. The following actual impacts related to
employees were assessed as material in the analysis under the double materiality principle:

        •    Building AI skills in the workforce empowers people to adapt to changing work requirements and take on
             new roles, which has a positive impact on their professional competitiveness, employability and career
             development.
        •    Promoting diversity and an inclusive corporate culture strengthens employees’ sense of belonging within
             the Company, increasing their motivation and loyalty.
        •    Low diversity in leadership positions, especially in terms of gender distribution, can demotivate
             underrepresented groups to aspire to leadership roles, inhibit career development and thus reduce
             opportunities to earn a higher salary, as customary in leadership positions.
        •    Flexible work in terms of working hours and location enables work-life balance and is conducive to
             employee health, satisfaction and long-term loyalty.
        •    Employees are actively involved in transformation processes through co-determination and participation.
             For example, in the event of organisational and technological changes, they are actively involved via the
             works council and other participation formats. Their interests are taken into account at an early stage in all
             major changes to enable a trust-based and socially acceptable transformation.

All employees of Scout24 SE and its subsidiaries within the scope of consolidation were included in the analysis –
regardless of whether they have a permanent or temporary contract or whether they are full-time or part-time
employees. The interests of trainees, students in cooperative education programmes, interns and working
students who do not fall under the definition of employees for the purposes of this report are represented and
taken into account by the People team and the works council. The perspective of non-employee workers was
included where corresponding data were available. No material impacts were identified with regard to non-
employees. The negative impact within the diversity topic has been identified as systemic. Unless otherwise
stated, no groups of employees were identified that are exposed to a higher risk of negative impacts due to certain
characteristics or activities. All impacts described apply equally to all employees. No material opportunities or risks
were identified. The assessment also considered the opportunities and risks that could arise from the impact with
respect to the Company.

The Leading European Digital Employer People Strategy comprises three pillars that cover the material impacts
and translate them into operational actions:

    1.   Increasing attractiveness and visibility as an employer through first-class employee experience and
         competitive total compensation packages in combination with targeted employer branding (with
         employee experience including the material topics of social dialogue and work-life balance)

    2.   Increasing organisational and individual performance through targeted talent management and
         development, agile and effective organisational structures and effective collaboration (covers the
         material topics of training and skills development)

    3.   Strengthening the corporate culture by exemplifying diversity, equity and inclusion in combination with
         inclusive leadership that is geared towards growth (covers the material topic of diversity)

To implement the ambitions for diversity, equity and inclusion in the third strategic pillar, a diversity, equity and
inclusion strategy (DEI strategy) was developed that in turn comprises three elements: inclusive corporate and
leadership culture, equitable talent processes and development, and value-driven business activities. The strategy
is available on the }Company’s website. The commitment to diversity, equity and inclusion is not only a
responsibility towards society, but in fact a strategic imperative that can have a strong influence on the Company’s
ability to innovate and on its overall success. A working environment that considers different perspectives,
encourages creativity and reflects the heterogeneous nature of society as a whole lays the foundations to enable
anticipating end-users’ needs and to thus contribute to sustainable corporate growth. Satisfied and well-qualified
staff as well as access to a diverse talent pool are key if we are to preclude potential negative effects on our
product development time plans. Due to their great importance for Scout24, both topics, diversity and training, are
anchored in its core values.

Policies related to own workforce (S1-1)
The People, Organisation & Culture team is responsible for HR matters throughout the Scout24 Group. The
Sustainability & DEI team is responsible for matters related to diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI). Both teams are
represented in the ELT through the leadership role of the Chief People & Sustainability Officer (CPSO), who reports
directly to the CEO. This joint management responsibility for people (own workforce) and sustainability interlinks
these topics strategically and operationally.

As the overarching policy in terms of }Business conduct policies and corporate culture, the Scout24 Code of
Conduct (}Code of Conduct) which is binding for all employees, sets out the Scout24 Group’s values and forms the
general framework for action. It also applies to business partners, suppliers and service providers and expressly
prohibits all forms of forced labour, child labour and human trafficking.

This central values policy above all is key to implementation of the people and DEI strategies and their material
actual impacts. The core values were revised in the 2025 reporting year. The previous values policy was updated in
the process, preserving its essence and focussing on the areas that are important for the Company’s future
success:

    •    Simplify: we are obsessed about simplification
         We remove complexity because it blocks scale, speed and customer experience. By constantly learning,
         we spark innovations to make hard decisions easy. We act with boldness.

The core values are part of the Code of Conduct and apply to all employees at all entities in the Scout24 Group.
They are an integral part of recruitment and onboarding processes, in regular feedback meetings and in
performance reviews. In addition to the People team, managers from various units of the Company and the works
council were involved in developing the values policy. The employees were involved by means of online surveys. In
terms of impacts, the values policy aims in particular to establish learning and development as a continuous
process and to promote diversity and an inclusive corporate culture.

In addition, further specific policies have been implemented for the material topics that concern employees, which
are monitored by the People team and the Sustainability & DEI team.

Training and skills development
To implement the second pillar of the people strategy (talent management and development), particularly with
regard to the material topics of training and skills development, a learning and development policy was
established in the reporting year that covers four areas: career development with flexible development paths, an AI
training programme to build digital skills, the training portfolio for targeted skills development, and open learning
formats for collaborative knowledge sharing. The conceptual approach is valid throughout the Company, and the
elements are introduced in stages at new subsidiaries.

Diversity
Supplementary to its own values policy, Scout24 has committed to comply with the United Nations Universal
Declaration of Human Rights, the Guidelines and Declaration of Principles of the International Labour Organization
(ILO), the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and the principles of the UNGC. These principles are
reflected in Scout24’s Code of Conduct and its policy statement on respect for human rights, the implementation
of which is the responsibility of the General Counsel in his/her additional capacity as Human Rights Officer. The
Sustainability & DEI, Compliance, Risk, People and Procurement teams manage human rights compliance within the
Company at an operational level, including monitoring and checking compliance with the above guidelines and
principles. By signing the Diversity Charter and the UN Women’s Empowerment Principles, Scout24 has also
committed itself to implementing the respective principles in the Company and strengthening the rights of women
in the workplace.

These commitments are also enshrined in the internal policy promoting diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI policy)
published in 2024, which applies to the employees of all subsidiaries in the Scout24 Group and covers the
principles, targets and actions for promoting DEI. The policy was developed jointly by the People, Sustainability &
DEI and Compliance teams with the involvement of the works councils. Scout24 takes a zero-tolerance approach
to any form of discrimination, harassment, threats or other hostile or abusive behaviour in the workplace. The same
applies to discrimination based on ethnic origin, skin colour, gender, age, religion, disability, marital status, sexual
orientation, nationality or any other personal characteristics. This applies equally to all employees without any
special commitment in favour of particular groups. In order to promote diversity and inclusion and to prevent and
curb discrimination, Scout24 relies on the awareness-raising and training formats provided for in the DEI policy that
are described in detail in the }Actions section.

Scout24’s commitments and processes in the area of human rights relate in particular to the impact in the field of
diversity and are described under }Business conduct policies and corporate culture. Employees from the
Sustainability & DEI, Compliance, People, Risk and Opportunity Management, Procurement and Sales teams are
represented in the internal working group on human rights.

Work-life balance
The company agreement on mobile working, which was updated in October 2025 to strengthen in-person
interactions within the team in line with the core value ‘Collaborate’, governs the topic of work-life balance. There
is also a company agreement for special leave in the event of specific personal events. Drawn up with the
involvement of the works council, both agreements apply to Scout24 SE and Immobilien Scout GmbH. The
Sprengnetter Group has its own policy on mobile working. All other subsidiaries apply regulations that allow a
certain number of mobile working days in their operational practice.

Social dialogue
In the area of co-determination and participation, a new IT framework agreement was concluded with the works
council of Scout24 SE and Immobilien Scout GmbH in the 2025 reporting year. It governs the works council’s
mandatory co-determination rights relating to the introduction, use and modification of lT systems in the Company
to ensure that employees’ protection needs, particularly with regard to personal privacy and data privacy, are
considered as well as the requirements of a modern corporate environment and the dynamic technological
developments. Due to ongoing centralisation, the IT systems subject to co-determination under the IT framework
agreement are also increasingly shaping the system landscapes at entities that are not represented by the works
council, given their undifferentiated Group-wide use.

The guidance and policies are available to employees on the intranet in German and English.

Processes for engaging with own workforce and workers’ representatives about impacts (S1-2)
Scout24 primarily uses digital, anonymised surveys as a method of involving employees with regard to the impacts.
The results of the surveys are also discussed with the works councils.

In the annual engagement surveys, employees at all entities are asked about what they expect from their working
environment and in relation to the material topics and how satisfied they are with Scout24. In particular, the actual
impacts related to training and skills development are addressed here. The Group-wide response rate was 79% in
2025 (2024: 85%). In addition, a short survey was conducted at the end of 2025, in which 75% of employees across
the Company took part. Based on the results, the CPSO will define appropriate actions with the involvement of the
ELT. These will be implemented by the People team, and their success will be measured in subsequent
engagement surveys. Moreover, the outcomes are discussed with the works council, and each team receives its
own feedback report to enable the adoption of internal measures in the team.

Regarding the revised core values, employees were involved through a separate survey and additionally asked for
feedback on their understanding, implementation and own contribution to the values in a short survey at the end of
the year.

An annual inclusion survey is conducted to obtain feedback specifically on the actual impacts related to work-life
balance and on the topic of diversity. The anonymous online survey provides insights into various aspects of
diversity at the Company and makes it possible to measure inclusion and analyse the perspective of potentially
marginalised groups of employees.

In addition to these surveys, employees are involved through company-wide and department-specific employee
meetings as well as regular team meetings. A specific survey on feedback to managers (upward feedback) is also
conducted annually. Individual feedback meetings for employees with their direct manager are held twice a year (}
Training and skills development metrics).

Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for own workers to raise concerns (S1-3)
With the principles of the people strategy, the core values and the DEI policy, the Company endeavours to avoid or
reduce negative impacts on employees and to take remedial action in the event of an incident.

Employees have various channels at their disposal if they wish to discuss any questions relating to the Code of
Conduct, report any violations or address any personal matters. Internally, they can approach the Compliance
department, their managers, the People team, the Sustainability & DEI team or the works council at entities that
have one. It is also possible to anonymously contact the external ombudsperson or use the whistle-blower system.
The processes and how whistle-blowers are protected are described in detail in the }Business conduct policies
and corporate culture section. Information about these points of contact is provided on the intranet, in the
mandatory DEI training, in compliance training as part of the onboarding process and in the DEI policy. The

objective is to resolve any potential or actual incidents respectfully, confidentially and swiftly, and with utmost
diligence.

As set out in the DEI policy, responsibility for dealing with reported incidents lies with the HR business partners in
the People team. They interview the persons involved and any individuals who might be able to shed light on the
matter and investigate the (suspected) incident. In consultation with the Compliance team, it is checked whether a
compliance violation has occurred that would be subject to the policy on consequence management. In the event
of actual employee misconduct, various disciplinary measures can be taken depending on the nature and severity
of the incident. If necessary, suitable means are used to provide support and accompany the person harmed. All
reported incidents are documented (}Incidents and complaints). Confidentiality is ensured throughout the entire
process.

In the annual inclusion survey, employees are asked anonymously whether they trust the reporting channels and
processes and feel safe to report potential misconduct. Any incidents reported, including any action taken or fines,
penalties or compensation payable, are documented, tracked in accordance with internal processes and the
results are monitored. The effectiveness of the measures is evaluated with the stakeholders involved; it was
concluded in the reporting period that no adjustments were necessary.

Taking action on material impacts on own workforce, and approaches to mitigating material risks
and pursuing material opportunities related to own workforce, and effectiveness of those actions
(S1-4)
To mitigate the identified negative impact related to diversity in leadership positions and to promote the positive
impacts related to work-life balance, training, participation and inclusive corporate culture, the Company draws on
the governance structure developed for HR matters, the strategy, policies and associated financial, human and
organisational resources. That is the basis on which the teams develop suitable actions. Information from
engagement with employees is also included in this process. Otherwise, by taking the measures described below,
the Company aims to avoid causing any further material negative impacts on its employees. Unless otherwise
stated, the actions focus on the Company’s own operations and the employees of the entire Scout24 Group. The
actions are generally ongoing and also planned for the future. The effectiveness of the actions is measured in
particular by the progress made towards the targets as well as through regular feedback from the workforce as
part of the employee surveys. At events and training sessions, participants are asked for feedback immediately
afterwards. Based on these findings, the actions implemented in relation to all topics are continuously updated
and adjusted as necessary during the year.

Training and skills development
To promote skills development, Scout24 offers specific training opportunities, particularly in the field of AI, as well
as encouraging regular feedback, support for managers and systematic succession planning. These measures
were implemented in stages at the new entities during the reporting year.

The following actions served to support the focus topic of ‘Building AI skills’ in 2025:

    •    An AI assistant was made available to all employees throughout the Group in spring 2025. Its launch was
         accompanied by events in German and English. A knowledge repository on the intranet offers permanent
         support and is supplemented by regular communication and application examples.
    •    In 2025, the annual Learning Day revolved around the topic of AI, offering a wide range of learning
         opportunities for different levels of experience.
    •    Staff in the IT department are regularly offered training courses on various AI applications specifically for
         programming. In addition, the Organisational Development team organises events on the topic of AI to
         support teams throughout the Company.
    •    A multi-stage internal AI training programme will be designed and made available to employees from the
         first half of 2026.
    •    Employees have the option to sign a declaration of consent if they also wish to use the AI application for
         private purposes.

There are further actions other than building AI skills that have been implemented on the basis of the learning and
development strategy:

Diversity
People can only perform at their best if they feel safe, appreciated and respected as individuals. It is important to
Scout24 to avoid infringing on the principles of equality from the outset and to contribute to greater diversity and
inclusion in society. To this end – and in addition to its updated core values, the internal DEI policy and the
grievance mechanisms – Scout24 places a particular emphasis on active support and prevention through
education. The Company publishes progress in the area of diversity in the annual DEI Report, which is available on
the }Company’s website.

The actions listed below are intended to strengthen the positive impacts of diversity and inclusion in the Company
and to respond to the lack of diversity in leadership positions and the resulting unadjusted gender pay gap. They
were also introduced in stages at the new entities in 2025.

    •    In internal training programmes, the focus is on promoting female talent. In the reporting year, 68% (2024:
         44%) of participants in the team leads training programme were women. A revised talent programme will
         be held in the first quarter of 2026.
    •    Managers at head-of level and above are required to set themselves one goal per year relating to
         diversity, equity and inclusion. This measure can be used to set sector-specific priorities for DEI initiatives
         and directly counter negative impacts.
    •    The core value of ‘true leadership’ as set out in the Code of Conduct provides managers with a clear
         framework for an inclusive and values-driven leadership culture. At the same time, all employees are
         encouraged to contribute to the corporate culture on the basis of these values.
    •    The regular DEI training programme for all employees includes mandatory training for new hires, Diversity
         Week with training on various aspects of DEI, and focus training sessions that the Sustainability & DEI team
         offers for internal teams, such as a foundations workshop for new subsidiaries or an anti-racism workshop.
    •    A partner of Annedore-Leber-Berufsbildungswerk vocational training centre, Scout24 offers young
         people with a disability the opportunity to complete the work experience phase of their training at the
         Company. In the 2025 reporting year, three (2024: three) trainees were employed through this initiative.

Additional actions serve to further raise awareness and provide training and possibilities for networking in relation
to the topic of diversity and inclusion in order to strengthen the positive impacts of the Group’s inclusive corporate
culture:

Work-life balance
The actions to promote the positive impacts of work-life balance mainly relate to the aspects of mobile work and
the provision of individual counselling services. Most of the actions have been implemented throughout the
Company.

    •    A hybrid work model offers the flexibility of mobile working while focussing on in-person collaboration in
         the office.
    •    The cooperation arrangement with a family service offers employees information, individual advice and
         support in different phases of life and in the event of family-related challenges. The family service has not
         yet been implemented in the Sprengnetter Group.
    •    A platform to promote work-life balance and mental health offers digital resources and events as well as
         anonymous individual counselling on professional and private challenges. Introduced in 2025, there is also
         the option to use individual coaching sessions. For the Sprengnetter Group, this platform will be made
         available from 2026.
    •    Introduced in 2024, the Company has trained first-aiders for mental health to assist colleagues in crises
         such as exceptional mental health situations or addiction problems and to organise further professional
         support if required.
    •    Mental health topics were additionally addressed in online presentations held for all employees, for
         example, on burnout prevention.

In addition, the following options are available to support a work-life balance:

    •    Employees (except in the Sprengnetter Group) can work from abroad for a certain period of time and
         under certain conditions.
    •    A parent-child office has been set up in the Berlin office.

Social dialogue
The works councils of Scout24 SE/Immobilien Scout GmbH and at the Cologne site of Propstack GmbH (formerly:
FLOWFACT GmbH) represent the interests of employees in accordance with the German Works Council
Constitution Act (‘Betriebsverfassungsgesetz’, BetrVG). The following actions in particular have been established
for this purpose: regular open consultation hours for employees, staff meetings, regular and ad-hoc exchanges
with the HR managers at entity level. The works council also provides information on employee rights regularly via
internal communication channels.

In addition, employees are involved in shaping transformation processes directly and through representation by
the works councils. In the reporting year 2025, they were involved mainly in relation to the AI transformation:

    •    The IT framework agreement was concluded with the works council (see }Policies related to own
         workforce).
    •    All employees were surveyed about AI on various occasions. In addition to specific use cases and the need
         for functionalities, the main topics discussed were access to training, trust in the responsible use of AI and
         employees’ concerns about replacing their own skills.
    •    As strategic focus topic, AI was regularly addressed at company meetings and other event formats in the
         reporting year. The internal communication platforms will provide a space to actively share application
         examples, best practices and lessons learned.

Targets related to managing material negative impacts, advancing positive impacts, and managing
material risks and opportunities (S1-5)
The corporate objectives concerning employees focus on reducing the negative impacts of the lack of diversity in
leadership positions, particularly with regard to gender distribution. In accordance with the DEI policy, Scout24
sets general diversity targets at Company level and with respect to leadership and succession planning. All targets
have been developed by the Sustainability & DEI team in collaboration with experts from the People team’s
specialist departments and have been approved by the Management Board. Information gained from engagement
with employees and employee representatives, for example, in the annual engagement and inclusion surveys, was
included in the process. The same applies to the identification of potential for improvement. Using the HR systems
and tools, the staff members responsible regularly review progress towards all the metrics specified in the targets.
The status is regularly reported to the ELT. There were no significant changes to metrics or measurement methods
in the reporting year. The scope of application was extended to all entities and – for women in leadership positions
– to all entities in the second year after consolidation.

The gender parity target is derived from the general diversity objectives set out in the DEI policy. Considering the

Through its actions geared to target achievement, Scout24 contributes to reducing inequalities in professional
development and in terms of career opportunities in society. This is achieved through the Company’s direct
influence on professional opportunities and support offered to (potential) employees and by serving as a role
model for employees and their families as well as for other companies. In the 2025 reporting year, Scout24 made
significant progress in this respect, but did not meet its ambitious targets. Scout24 will continue the initiated
actions and will purposefully develop them further in order to gradually realise the improvements it is aiming for.

For building AI skills in the workforce, there was no measurable target yet in the reporting year. A Workforce AI
Upskilling Index will be developed in the course of 2026 as a key metric to measure the skills employees acquire in
the field of AI.

No measurable targets have been defined in accordance with ESRS for the three material topics that have a
positive impact relating to co-determination and participation, work-life balance and inclusive corporate culture.
The effectiveness of the policies is verified through engagement with employees. The primary processes used are
the engagement survey and the inclusion survey, which are conducted once a year and measure employees’
perceptions, both qualitatively and quantitatively (see }Processes for engaging with own workforce).

Training and skills development metrics (S1-13)
In the reporting period, an average of 11.9 (2024: 8.7) hours of training were completed per employee. In 2025, men
completed an average of 11.2 (2024: 7.6) hours of training, women 12.8 (2024: 10.1) hours.

Two formal feedback meetings (MyDialogue) are scheduled for all employees each year. In the 2025 reporting year,
89.1% (2024: 79.6%) of employees took part in at least one feedback meeting (88.7% of men and 89.5% of women;
2024: 80.3% of men and 78.7% of women). On average, 1.6 (2024: 1.4) interviews took place per person.

Methodology: training and skills development
The training hours reported relate to the full year 2025, calculated as an average for the employees working at the Company on 31 December 2025
(S1-6). For calculation purposes, the number of hours of training was divided by the total employee population (S1-6) or the number of employees
by gender (S1-6). The data include training figures available from internal and external training courses as well as content from the digital
Scout24Academy and the Sprengnetter Online Campus. For training courses for which no personal data is available due to data privacy reasons
(participation via Zoom), the disaggregation by gender was estimated according to the gender percentages in the Company (S1-6). For the
percentage of feedback meetings, all employees who had at least one meeting documented in the HR systems in 2025 were counted as of
31 December 2025 and divided by the total employee population (S1-6). For the average number of meetings per person, the total number of
meetings was divided by the total employee population (S1-6). As the interviews take place in defined periods, newly hired employees do not take
part in all of them, depending on their starting date. Some of the new subsidiaries acquired were integrated into the process during the year.
Employees who have not specified their gender are not included in the metric disaggregated by gender for data protection reasons.



Work-life balance metrics (S1-15)
All employees at the entities in all countries are entitled by law to take family-related leave. In 2025, 75 (2024: 88)
employees were on parental leave (6.8% of the workforce; 2024: 8.3%). A share of 44.0% (2024: 33.0%) of employees
on parental leave were fathers; 56.0% (2024: 67.0%) were mothers. The number of women on maternity leave was 23
(2024: 25) in the reporting year. Four employees (2024: none) took leave to provide care to a relative.

Methodology: work-life balance
The information on leave for family reasons relates to the full year 2025. All employees on leave of absence for at least one day in the 2025
reporting year were counted. To calculate the percentage, this number is divided by the total employee population (S1-6).

Remuneration metrics (pay gap and total remuneration) (S1-16)
The gender pay gap indicates the percentage by which the average gross hourly earnings of women are lower than
those of men. The unadjusted gender pay gap for the entire scope of consolidation is 21.0% for the 2025 reporting
year. This figure is primarily a consequence of the demographic structure of the Company, particularly the
distribution of female and male employees at different hierarchical levels. The unadjusted pay gap does not take
into account structural differences such as function or professional experience. In order to illustrate potential
differences in compensation for comparable jobs, the adjusted gender pay gap is considered. For the entities
analysed, the adjusted gender pay gap for 2025 was 1.1%. The underlying calculation method is currently only
applicable to Scout24 SE and Immobilen Scout GmbH (around 57% of all employees in the Group). There are plans to
extend it to other subsidiaries.

The ratio of the annual total remuneration of the highest-paid individual to the median of all employees is 45.1:1 for
the 2025 reporting year.

Methodology: remuneration metric
The unadjusted gender pay gap is calculated on the basis of the gross hourly earnings of all employees as of 31 December 2025 in accordance with
S1-6. The following are taken into account, in each case as of 31 December 2025: basic salary, bonus for 100% target achievement, mobility benefits
(company car or company car allowance, public transport or other mobility allowances) and long-term incentives (allocation amount in 2025).
Company pensions are reflected either with reference to the contribution paid in a defined contribution plan or, in the case of an employer-
subsidised gross deferred compensation plan, with reference to the employer subsidy that can be paid if the employee accepts the offer. The
following formula was used for the calculation: (average gross hourly earnings of male employees - average gross hourly earnings of female
employees) ÷ average gross hourly earnings of male employees × 100. Employees who have not specified their gender are not included in the
calculation for data protection reasons.
The adjusted gender pay gap is calculated on the same basis, but also includes hierarchical levels and functions to enable comparability of the job
profiles. The pay gap is calculated for each job profile using the above formula, taking into account the above-mentioned compensation
components. The results are weighted by calculating the percentage deviation per position, multiplying this by the total number in the relevant
profile and adding it up for the total number of people. This procedure is currently applicable to Scout24 SE and Immobilien Scout GmbH. Further
companies will be successively integrated into the underlying job structure in future and subsequently included in the calculation.
The same compensation components are used in calculating the ratio of the annual total remuneration of the highest-paid individual to the
median of all employees (excluding the highest-paid individual). The analysis is based on gross annual salaries on a full-time basis. The calculation
divides the annual total remuneration of the highest-paid individual by the median of the annual total remuneration of all employees (excluding
the highest-paid individual) in accordance with S1-6.

Consumers and end-users (ESRS S4)
Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with strategy and business model
(SBM-3)
As the foundation of its corporate strategy and business model as a data-driven technology company, the
Company processes personal and property-related data. Data security is therefore a high priority and forms the
basis for end-users’ trust in the Group’s products and services. This means that business success also depends to a
large extent on the security of the Scout24 Group’s digital marketplaces. It is the Company’s aim and, at the same
time, a commitment on the part of the Company to handle the data collected, captured, stored or used in a
responsible manner and adhere to all laws relevant for data protection at the Scout24 Group. The goals are to rule
out, by means of internal processes and structures, any misuse or loss of data through unauthorised access to
personal data and information, to avoid damage and losses to individuals and safeguard the right to informational
self-determination.

The potential negative impacts identified by the Company in the area of privacy and personal data protection on
end-users include above all the risk of cybercrime. Fake listings or ‘advance payment fraud’ can cause financial
losses to end-users and lead to a loss of trust. This negative impact can affect the entire range of the Scout24
Group's services and products offered as well as all end-users, even in the case of isolated incidents. No groups of

By providing extensive and transparent information on the housing market, the Company also generates positive

democratising real estate data that was previously only available to professionals. This results in more informed
and fairer real estate transactions for end-users.

Furthermore, innovations related to artificial intelligence can have a positive impact on user satisfaction and lead
to more efficient property decisions, as AI-based product functions on ImmoScout24 platforms improve the
quality and relevance of property information for end-users, shorten search times through more precise matching
of supply and demand and increase the likelihood of a successful property transaction.

In addition, there is a potentially positive impact for the Scout24 Group end-users from new products related to the
sustainability requirements in the real estate industry. Scout24 is working on solutions that transparently present,
for example, climate risks, energy efficiency and renovation requirements. Such digital tools and training options
can help homeowners to make more informed and sustainable decisions to increase their property’s climate
resilience.

Policies related to consumers and end-users (S4-1)
Scout24 is fundamentally aware of its corporate responsibility and is committed to preventing or minimising
negative impacts on human rights, including in relation to end-users, in its own operations and along the entire
supply chain. To this end, the Group adopted a }Policy statement on respect for human rights in 2024 and
updated it in 2025. A }grievance mechanism has been in place since 2024. Further information on the processes
and mechanisms for monitoring and respecting human rights are described in the Governance section
under }Policies. For 2025 and the previous year, there were no indications of human rights violations in our own
operations or in the value chain. Should the Scout24 Group become aware of any failure to meet human rights
obligations, it would immediately take appropriate remedial action, taking into account the interests of end-users.
Such action aims to prevent or end any instance of non-respect or minimise its extent.

Climate change adaptation
The integration of modernisation calculators for properties on the ImmoScout24 platform is relevant for the user
group of homeowners and prospective buyers. They can encourage this target group to make more sustainable
decisions and increase the climate resilience of properties in the long term.

The existing product policy continued to apply in 2025. The policy further aims to create awareness among
homeowners of the need for modernisation and the associated costs and to integrate an informative product
offering for buyers and homeowners on the ImmoScout24 platform. Implementation is monitored by the
respective product managers through continuous measurement of key metrics. The policy’s scope of application
covers the Company’s own operations with a focus on homeowners and prospective buyers and, due to lead
generation for third parties, the downstream value chain in Germany and Austria. The highest level of operational
responsibility within the Company is the Vice President Product Management, who reports directly to the Chief
Product Officer in the ELT.

Data protection and information security
In the materiality analysis, one positive impact and one negative impact for end-users were rated as material with
regard to data protection and information security:

    •   Positive: the implementation of improved data protection and IT security standards reduces the risk of
        data leaks and cyberattacks, increasing end-users’ and customers’ trust in the secure processing of their
        personal and property data on Scout24 platforms. This increases their willingness to use the platforms and
        leads to a higher level of data protection compliance.
    •   Negative: as digital real estate platforms, Scout24’s marketplaces are exposed to cybersecurity threats
        that can cause financial or personal damage or loss to end-users and customers, in particular through
        prepayment fraud using fake property listings and the misuse of personal data. This can reduce trust in
        digital property services with lasting effect.

Scout24’s data protection policy is based on three relevant guidelines. Their purpose is to avoid material negative
impacts arising from a personal data and privacy breach. They are aimed at all members of staff as well as at
freelancers and external providers who have access to data of the Scout24 Group or are responsible for such data.
Data protection is the responsibility of the Management Board. At an operational level, the Legal department
manages the internal data protection organisation. Employees have access to the aforementioned policies and
documents via Scout24’s intranet or via the compliance officers at the subsidiaries. Unless indicated otherwise, the
policies apply to the entire Scout24 Group.

The internal data protection policy is intended to guarantee that all processing operations within the Scout24
Group relating to personal data are in compliance with the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation
(GDPR) and the respective applicable local regulations of data protection legislation in the individual member
states. This applies to all entities of the Scout24 Group in which Scout24 SE, directly or indirectly, holds a majority
(>50%) and to investees over which Scout24 SE, directly or indirectly, has the power to direct their activities. To this
end, it gives employees practical guidance on how to implement data protection. In addition to the policy, an
instruction has been issued on how to deal with data protection incidents. This sets out specific actions that
employees in the Group must take in order to report possible incidents to the responsible data protection
authority within 72 hours and inform the data subjects. Responsibility for implementing the policy is assumed by
the respective teams, functional units and entities of the Scout24 Group. The Group-wide governance structure
related to data protection serves to monitor implementation of the policy.

To support implementation of the corporate data protection policy, Scout24 has set out in the publicly accessible
Data Protection Code of Conduct the guiding principles of entrepreneurial action in terms of data protection,
transparency, necessity of the processed data and data minimisation for all relevant addressees. The Data
Protection Code of Conduct sets out specific work instructions for how to act in accordance with data protection
requirements. The policy states that personal and confidential data is used and processed exclusively within the
permitted framework in order to protect the data subject’s right to informational self-determination. The }Data
Protection Code of Conduct can be accessed on Scout24’s website.

The information security policy aims to protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of Scout24’s data and
information systems. The policy provides the framework for setting strategic objectives for information security at
the Scout24 Group and ensures that the activities of the information security management system comply with
legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, with a focus on the commitment to continuous improvement. It
applies to all information systems, employees and processes of Scout24 and all subsidiaries within the scope of
consolidation except for the Sprengnetter Group. The Management Board and the ELT are responsible for
implementing and monitoring the information security policy, which governs Scout24’s approach to security and
ensures best security practices. The policy is based on the international standard ISO/IEC 27001. It was developed
taking into account the interests and concerns of key stakeholders, especially customers and employees. The
policy can be accessed by all employees via the internal Scout24 compliance management system and is regularly
monitored and reviewed as part of internal audits. Information security is also integrated in Scout24’s company-
wide risk and opportunity management system. Internal processes and policies are adapted as necessary in line
with the changes.

The Sprengnetter Group has its own information security management system (ISMS) with its own policies. The
ISMS covers actions in the areas of organisational, personal, physical and technological security. Core elements
include the management of information assets and their classification, access control and identity management,
security checks on personnel, physical security measures and technical protection measures such as vulnerability
management, data backups and secure software development. The Sprengnetter Group has also established
processes to manage security incidents as well as business continuity measures. The system is supported by
regular internal audits, risk assessments and continuous improvement processes. The Sprengnetter Group's
management is responsible for implementing and monitoring the information security policy. In September 2024,
Sprengnetter GmbH and Sprengnetter Property Valuation Finance GmbH obtained ISO/IEC 27001:2022
certification. For Scout24 SE and ImmoScout24 in Germany as well as bulwiengesa GmbH, the aim is to achieve
corresponding certification by the end of 2026. The other entities in the consolidation scope are to follow in 2027.

Access to quality information
End-users should be able to make their decision to rent, buy, sell, let or finance a property on the basis of
transparent information about the property market. With this in mind, the Scout24 Group’s operations aim to
provide market data and quality information to all players in the real estate market. This understanding of the
Company’s purpose is also reflected in the business and growth strategy for the Scout24 Group with a clear
emphasis on interconnectivity (}Fundamentals of the Group). Data are provided across the entire product range

positive impact.

In its materiality analysis, the Scout24 Group rated the effects of the use of artificial intelligence as a positive
impact, in that AI-based product functions on ImmoScout24 platforms can help improve the quality and relevance
of property information for end-users, shorten search times and increase the likelihood of successful property
transactions, which can lead to higher user satisfaction and more efficient real estate decisions.

Artificial intelligence is an integral element of the }Corporate strategy. The declared aim is to offer users a
personalised experience along the entire real estate value chain – from property searches and transactions to
management and modernisation. The internal AI policy governs how artificial intelligence is used at the Scout24
Group. Its objective is to define internal regulations and framework conditions for responsible, ethical and
effective use of artificial intelligence, always ensuring compliance with legal requirements, particularly in terms of
data protection law and intellectual property rights. An AI system includes both commercial and internally
developed AI software as well as web-based AI applications. This definition primarily encompasses AI systems
within the meaning of the EU’s AI Regulation (2024/1689). These include tools and applications that increase
internal productivity by supporting employees in their tasks, as well as AI-based applications that are developed to
improve customer experience and product usage. Scout24 expressly prohibits all AI practices that are prohibited
under Art. 5 of the EU’s AI Regulation. These include, among others, the use of AI systems that manipulate behaviour
through subliminal or deceptive techniques or apply unjustified social scoring. In addition, the policy regulates the
internal practices for the procurement and testing of AI systems, as well as the duties of all employees with regard
to the critical review of AI output and compliance with the legal provisions on data protection, information security
and protecting the confidentiality of information. Compliance with this policy is monitored by the Compliance
department (through sample testing in some cases). Any violations are assessed and dealt with in accordance with
the provisions of the consequence management policy. The most senior person with operational responsibility for
the use of artificial intelligence is Scout24’s Chief Technology Officer, who reports directly to the Management
Board.

Processes for engaging with consumers and end-users about impacts (S4-2)
The processes described below serve to involve end-users in general and in relation to the material positive actual
impacts related to climate change adaptation, market transparency and the use of artificial intelligence.

The satisfaction of our private and professional end-users is determined on an ongoing basis by means of online
surveys on the websites and in the apps. More than 25,000 survey responses were analysed in 2025 (2024: 28,000).
Respondents were asked about functionalities and potential for improvement. Responsibility for such surveys and
for processing the feedback is assigned to the Product teams. In addition, feedback is obtained from the
Company’s Sales team’s direct interactions with professional customers. Private end-users mainly contact the
Customer Care team. Monthly analyses of the net promoter score, the customer satisfaction score and rating items
developed in-house are carried out on the basis of the aforementioned surveys. For example, end-users are asked
to rate how trustworthy they consider ImmoScout24 to be. Respondents also have the option to leave comments.
The results are evaluated on a monthly basis and presented to the Management Board as required. Operational
responsibility for customer satisfaction rests with the Customer Care, Product Management and Sales teams.

The Sprengnetter Group obtains feedback from its professional customers primarily through personal
engagement. Surveys are also conducted in individual areas as required, for example, on satisfaction or on possible
product improvements.

Twice a year, additional surveys are conducted among consumers specifically on the topic of data protection and
data security on ImmoScout24. One of the aims of the surveys is to gain insights into the perception of security and
experiences with fraud on the ImmoScout24 platform. Questions also concern the awareness of security measures.
End-users also have the opportunity to suggest measures to further improve the security precautions on the
platform. In the reporting year, the user surveys were accessible in the website’s search flow and in the
ImmoScout24 app during the two-week survey periods in May and November. In 2025, a total of 1,647 home seekers

Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for consumers and end-users to raise
concerns (S4-3)
Data protection
Cybersecurity threats and the misuse of personal data can result in material negative impact for end-users. End-
users of Scout24’s platforms can obtain information at any time on the websites of the Company and the
subsidiaries about which personal data are collected by the entities and how they are processed. Scout24 Group
transfers personal data to third parties on valid legal bases in accordance with the GDPR. End-users are informed
transparently about how their data are processed. This also includes the sale of leads to business partners as part
of the platform services, which is based on the users’ express consent. All end-users have the right to request the
erasure of personal data under the conditions set forth in Art. 17 GDPR at any time. Unless stated otherwise in the
data privacy statement, personal data is stored only for as long as necessary to achieve the purpose stated in the
data privacy statement or as prescribed within the framework of a statutory storage period. Thereafter, the data in
question is routinely blocked or completely erased or anonymised in accordance with the law. In the event of a
complaint, there are various ways to contact us – in person, by phone or using the email address provided in the
data protection information. End-users can also contact the responsible Customer Care team.

When data protection enquiries are received, these are answered by the relevant Customer Care department of
the subsidiaries. At Sprengnetter Group, this is assigned to the data protection coordinators. In the other
subsidiaries, the data protection coordinators are involved in more complex issues. Depending on the case in
question, the Group’s data protection officer may also respond to enquiries.

Scout24 was in contact with the relevant supervisory authority in connection with various matters in the reporting
period. The processes are monitored continuously, and the potential for improvement is examined. The use of the
contact channels offered and enquiries received via the aforementioned reporting channels confirm their
effectiveness and end-users’ trust in them.

If they suspect scam listings on the Scout24 Group’s portals, end-users always have the option to report suspicious
listings or to contact the relevant Customer Care team by email. All enquiries received are documented. Anyone
who has been a victim of fraud receives information about secure account settings and how to avoid falling victim
on internet platforms. When the authorities have been contacted, the Company also closely supports them in their
investigations to the extent possible. Depending on the case at hand, end-users who have been victims of phishing
are guided through various support measures. Affected end-user accounts are blocked, and the end-users are
informed accordingly. Once verification has been completed, password protection is renewed. Depending on the
scenario, bookings and payment options are checked and cancelled or reactivated as appropriate. Further
information beyond the security processes is available on the website }sicherheit.immobilienscout24.de.
Questions received from end-users are answered here; scams are explained; and contact persons are named. In
addition, the general public’s attention is drawn to these issues by sharing tips and advice with the media and on
social media. The }User survey on data protection and security is used to obtain additional feedback from
ImmoScout24 users on their trust in the platform and awareness of the security precautions.

To ensure the effectiveness of the aforementioned processes for involving end-users, the Scout24 Group also has
a whistle-blower protection system that can be used confidentially and anonymously by internal and external
stakeholders. To standardise the systems, the Sprengnetter Group discontinued its existing whistle-blower system
in December 2025 and has since been integrated into the Scout24 Group’s system. Further information on whistle-
blower protection can be found in the Governance section under }Policies.
